title: Open question on Theorem 1.2 with $L=1$
statement_text: We do not know whether the following holds with $L=1$: for all $k,r$, there exist $L,C\ge1$ such that if $G$ admits a tree-decomposition $(T,(B_t:t\in V(T)))$ such that for each $t\in V(T)$, $B_t$ is the union of at most $k$ sets each with diameter at most $r$ in $G$, then $G$ admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with tree-width at most $k$.
context_text: Graphs may be infinite, and $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)$ is the number of edges of a shortest $u$–$v$ path in $G$ ($\infty$ if none). The diameter of $X\subseteq V(G)$ in $G$ is the maximum of $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)$ over $u,v\in X$. For $L,C\ge0$, a map $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry if $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)+C$ whenever $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)$ is finite, $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))+C$ whenever $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))$ is finite, and every vertex of $H$ is at distance at most $C$ from $\phi(V(G))$; with $L=1$ it is called additive. Tree-decompositions may be indexed by infinite trees. Berger and Seymour proved that if $G$ is connected and has a tree-decomposition whose bags all have diameter at most $r$ in $G$, then $G$ admits a $(1,6r+1)$-quasi-isometry to a tree. The authors extend this to bounded tree-width: for all $k,r$ there exist $L,C\ge1$ such that if $G$ has a tree-decomposition each of whose bags is the union of at most $k$ sets of diameter at most $r$ in $G$, then $G$ admits an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a graph with tree-width at most $k$ (the tree-width bound $k$ cannot be lowered to $k-1$). They remark that calling this an extension of the Berger–Seymour result is something of a stretch, since they do not know whether one can take $L=1$. For path-decompositions (and line-decompositions, the extension of path-decompositions to infinite graphs indexed by linearly ordered sets) they can take $L=1$, using a result from a companion paper.
notes: Stated as a parenthetical remark in the introduction rather than a labelled conjecture/question environment. Only the first 4000 characters of the introduction were provided; additional open problems later in the paper may not be captured.
